notes.b: The Consumer Rights Act 2022 gives consumers statutory rights (rights set by law) and remedies when they buy goods, services or digital content from traders. It applies to contracts made on or after 29 November 2022 and replaced the earlier law on sales and services for consumer contracts.
points: A trader is a person who supplies goods, services or digital content in the course of business, so the Act applies to shops, online sellers and service providers alike.
A consumer is an individual acting for purposes that are not part of their business, so someone buying a washing machine for their home is a consumer.
Statutory rights apply automatically to every contract between a trader and a consumer, whether or not the trader mentions them.
A trader cannot remove statutory rights through terms and conditions, small print or notices; a 'no refunds' sign does not override the Act.

Digital content, such as downloaded software, music or films, is covered by the same standards of quality, fitness and description as goods, because it is bought in the same way and can be just as faulty.
notes.tip: Name the Act as the Consumer Rights Act 2022 and give its idea in one line: it decides what a consumer can claim when a purchase is faulty. Keep it apart from the Consumer Protection Act 2007, which is about how traders behave.

notes.b: Goods must meet four standards at the time they are supplied, and the consumer is entitled to all of them whatever the trader says.
points: Satisfactory quality: goods must be of a standard a reasonable person would consider satisfactory, taking account of price and description. This includes being durable, safe, free from minor defects, and having an acceptable appearance and finish.

Fit for purpose: goods must be fit for the purposes for which goods of that type are normally used, and for any particular purpose the buyer made known to the trader, for example asking for a coat that is waterproof.
As described: goods must match any description given by the trader, the label or the advertisement, so a 'leather' bag that is plastic does not meet this right.
Correspond to sample or model: goods must match a sample or model shown to the consumer before purchase.
A fault that is present when the goods are supplied is the trader's responsibility, even if it appears only later.
The retailer is responsible for faulty goods and must deal with the complaint, even if the fault was made by the manufacturer. The consumer approaches the trader, not the manufacturer.
notes.tip: When asked how the law protects a buyer, name each right (satisfactory quality, fit for purpose, as described, match sample) and add a short explanation, for example durable, safe and free of defects. Say the retailer is responsible, not the manufacturer.

notes.b: A service is measured against what a competent provider would deliver and against what the trader said or agreed, so the consumer is protected even though there is no physical product to inspect.
points: Reasonable care and skill: a service must be carried out with the care and skill a competent provider would show, in other words to a high standard by a suitably qualified person.
Materials: any materials used in a service must be of satisfactory quality and fit for their purpose, so a repair using poor parts is a breach even if the work itself was careful.
Time: where no time was agreed, the service must be carried out within a reasonable time, so a trader cannot leave a job half-finished for months.
Price: where no price was agreed in advance, the consumer pays only a reasonable price for the service, which protects them from an inflated bill afterwards.
Matching what was said or agreed: the service must match what the trader told the consumer or agreed with them.
notes.tip: For a faulty service, cover all three: care and skill (high standard, qualified person), good materials, then the remedy. Marks go to each named right plus a short explanation.

notes.h: Remedies under the Consumer Rights Act 2022
notes.b: When goods or services do not meet their statutory standard, the remedies are applied in a set order: the consumer starts with the gentlest fix and moves to the next only if that fails.
points: First remedy for goods: repair or replacement at the trader's cost, within a reasonable time and without significant inconvenience to the consumer.
Second remedy for goods: a price reduction or a refund, where repair or replacement is not possible, is not carried out within a reasonable time, or causes significant inconvenience.

Short-term right to reject: the time limit for rejecting faulty goods outright is 30 days, so they can be rejected within 30 days of supply (delivery) and the consumer receives a full refund, without having to accept a repair first.
Services that are not performed to the required standard must be repeated by the trader, or the consumer can ask for a price reduction.

A manufacturer's guarantee is extra to statutory rights and cannot reduce them. A statutory right is set by law and applies automatically, whereas a guarantee is a voluntary promise from the manufacturer.
notes.tip: In a scenario, decide whether the consumer is entitled to anything, name the right that was broken, then give the remedy in order: repair or replacement, then price reduction or refund. You may also be asked to explain the difference between a statutory right and a guarantee.

notes.h: When statutory rights do not apply
notes.b: The Act protects buyers from faulty goods and services, not from every disappointment, so exam scenarios often turn on spotting when no remedy is owed.
points: There is no statutory right to a refund merely because the buyer changed their mind or dislikes the colour. Any refund, exchange or credit note in that case is the shop's own policy, a favour rather than a legal duty.
Goods bought in a sale are covered by the same statutory rights as goods bought at full price, so a sale does not weaken the consumer's position.
Exception: a fault that the trader pointed out before the sale is not covered by the statutory rights for that fault.
A consumer who was not told of a fault before purchase keeps the full statutory remedies for it.
Misuse or ordinary wear and tear is not a fault for which the trader is liable, because the goods were not faulty when supplied.
Proof of purchase, such as a receipt, bank statement or order confirmation, is needed to show the goods came from this trader.
notes.tip: In a refund scenario, first ask whether the goods are faulty or the buyer simply changed their mind. A fault gives a statutory remedy; a change of mind gives only whatever the shop's own policy allows.

notes.h: Consumer Protection Act 2007: unfair commercial practices
notes.b: The Consumer Protection Act 2007 is about how traders behave in advertising, pricing and selling, rather than what can be claimed for a faulty purchase. It prohibits unfair commercial practices and protects consumers from false and misleading claims, and it replaced the Consumer Information Act 1978.
points: Misleading actions: giving false or deceptive information about a product, its price, its origin or the trader's identity, which could lead a consumer to buy something they would not otherwise choose.
Misleading omissions: leaving out or hiding material information that a consumer needs in order to make a decision.
Aggressive practices: harassment, coercion, undue influence or pressure that limits the consumer's freedom to choose.
Prohibited practices: a list of practices banned in all cases, such as falsely claiming that a product has an approval it does not have, or using a quality mark without permission.
The Act is enforced by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC), which investigates and can prosecute offences. It does not settle an individual consumer's dispute with a trader.
The consumer benefits from protection against false advertising, honest price information, and a state body that takes action.
notes.tip: If asked to describe the protection of the Consumer Protection Act 2007, cover false or misleading claims about goods, services and price (including previous prices and recommended retail prices), then enforcement by the CCPC.

notes.h: Consumer Protection Act 2007: misleading price claims
notes.b: Price claims must be accurate, including claims about reductions and comparisons, because a price is often what persuades a consumer to buy.
points: False or misleading information about the price of goods or services is prohibited.
A claimed previous price or a claimed reduction must be accurate; a false or misleading reduction, such as a 'was' price the item never sold at, is an unfair practice.
A recommended retail price must not be used misleadingly to suggest a saving the consumer would not in fact make.
notes.tip: Name all three price points: false prices, false previous price or reduction, and a recommended retail price used to suggest a saving that does not exist.

keyTerms.definition: A person who supplies goods, services or digital content in the course of business.
A right given by law that applies automatically to a contract and cannot be removed by the trader's terms.
The standard that goods should be durable, safe, free from minor defects and acceptable in appearance and finish.
The standard that goods must be suitable for their usual use, or for a particular purpose made known to the trader.
Data produced and supplied in digital form, such as downloaded software, music or films.
A commercial practice in which material information that a consumer needs is left out, so that the consumer decides wrongly.
A commercial practice that uses harassment, coercion, undue influence or pressure to limit a consumer's freedom to choose.
A remedy in which the consumer pays less for goods or services that do not meet the statutory standard.

factCards.term: Order of remedies for faulty goods
factCards.definition: Repair or replacement first; a price reduction or refund if these are not possible or fail.

factCards.term: Four standards that goods must meet
factCards.definition: Satisfactory quality, fitness for purpose, matching the description, and matching any sample or model.

factCards.term: Time limit for rejecting faulty goods outright
factCards.definition: Within 30 days of supply, faulty goods can be rejected and the consumer receives a full refund.

factCards.term: Two types of misleading price information forbidden by the Consumer Protection Act 2007
factCards.definition: False or misleading information about the price itself, and false or misleading information about previous prices or recommended retail prices.

factCards.term: Categories of practice the Consumer Protection Act 2007 treats as unfair
factCards.definition: Misleading actions, misleading omissions, aggressive practices, and practices prohibited outright.

questions.prompt: Explain how the Consumer Rights Act 2022 protects a consumer who buys an appliance that develops a fault shortly after purchase.
questions.model: Goods must be of satisfactory quality and fit for purpose when supplied, and a fault present at supply is the trader's responsibility even if it appears later. The consumer can require repair or replacement at the trader's cost, within a reasonable time and without significant inconvenience. If repair or replacement is not possible or is not carried out, the consumer can take a price reduction or refund. Within 30 days of supply the consumer can reject the faulty appliance and receive a full refund. Statutory rights cannot be removed by a sign or the terms of sale.

questions.prompt: Discuss the statutory rights a consumer has when buying services under the Consumer Rights Act 2022, and explain how the Consumer Protection Act 2007 protects consumers against misleading price claims.
questions.model: Services: the consumer is entitled to a service performed with reasonable care and skill, using materials of satisfactory quality and fit for purpose, within a reasonable time where none was agreed, and at a reasonable price where none was agreed. If the service is not performed to standard, the consumer can require it to be performed again, or obtain a price reduction. These rights apply automatically and cannot be excluded by the trader's terms. Consumer Protection Act 2007: the Act forbids false or misleading information about goods, services and prices. A trader may not claim a previous price or a reduction that is untrue, and may not use a recommended retail price misleadingly to suggest a saving. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission enforces the Act and can investigate and prosecute offences. A complete answer distinguishes the contract rights given to the consumer from the advertising and pricing controls that protect consumers before purchase.
